2. The petitioner as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 278 of 1979 for a declaration that eviction proceeding under Eviction case No 6 of 1978-79 and all orders passed there-under are illegal, void and without jurisdiction and for permanent injunction restraining the defendants 1 to 4 from evicting the plaintiffs and proforma defendants 5 to 7 or in any way disturbing with their peaceful possession in the shop rooms in suit. After the filing of the suit the plaintiffs also filed an application for temporary injunction against the defendants Nos. 1 to 4. Defendants 1 and 2 filed a written statement in the suit denying the title and possession of the plaintiffs. They also filed written objection against the plaintiffs' prayer for temporary injunction. The learned Munsif rejected the plaintiffs' prayer for temporary injunction and held that plaintiffs prima facie right, title and possession in the suit land, the same being non-retainable land and having vested in the Government under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The learned Munsif also held that the suit was barred by res judicata. Against the mid order of the learned Munsif the plaintiffs preferred an appeal being Misc. Appeal No. 105 of 1980. The leaned Sub-ordinate Judge who heard the appeal held that the question whether the suit was barred by res judicata was a question relating to the merits and this should be decided at the time of hearing of the suit itself. He also considered that the Sub-Divisional Officer was not the competent authority to issue an eviction notice and that the plaintiff's predecessor was a tenant and not a rent-receiver. He also found that 30 days clear notice was necessary before eviction and this was not done. As such the learned Subordinate Judge held that the plaintiffs have made out a good prima facie case for injunction. He also found that the balance of 'convenience' was also in favour of the plaintiffs. As such, he granted the plaintiff's prayer for temporary injunction during pendeney of the suit after reversing the order of learned Munsif. As against the said order of the learned Subordinate Judge the contesting defendants moved the learned District Judge under section 115(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure and a rule was issued him. The learned District Judge by his judgement and order dated 15.7.80 allowed the revision and set aside the judgment and order of the learned Subordinate Judge and restored the order of the learned Munsif. Against the said order of the learned District Judge the present rule has been obtained. 

 4. From a perusal of section 21 we find that in cases where the Subordinate Judge has passed a decree or an order in original matter, appeal would lie to the District Judge where the value of the original suit in which, or in any proceeding arising out of which, the decree or order was made, did not exceed Tk. 20,000/-. This, obviously, is with regard to the original decree or original order passed by the learned Subordinate Judge. Section 21(1) states that in other cases the appeal from a decree or order of a Subordinate Judge would lie to the High Court Division. So, it has been categorically stated in this sub-section that all appeals shall lie to the District Judge excepting those not covered by section 21(1) of the Civil Courts Act. Section 21(4) is to the effect that the High Court Division may, with the previous sanction of the Government made by Notification in the Official Gazette, direct that appeals lying to the District Judge under sub-section (2) from all or any of the decrees of any Munsif shall be preferred to the court of such Subordinate Judge as may be mentioned in the notification and the appeals shall thereupon be preferred accordingly. No such notification has been filed to show that the instant appeal before us was notified to be filed before any Subordinate Judge or that any Subordinate Judge of the said District was ever authorised by any notification within the scope of section 21(4) of the Civil Courts Act to entertain any appeal. As such, appeal against the order passed by the Munsif was to be entertained by the District Judge and not by a Subordinate Judge. Chapter IV deals with the Special Jurisdiction of the Court. Section 22 of the Civil Court Act is to the following effect: 

 5. From a reading of section 22 we find that the District Judge can transfer any appeal pending before him from the decree or order of the Munsif to any Subordinate Judge under his administrative control. The District Judge has also power to withdraw any appeal from any court of Subordinate Judge and transfer it to some other court under his administrative control competent to dispose it of or he can himself hear and dispose of the same. Sub-section (3) is to the effect that the appeals transferred under section 22 shall be disposed of subject to rules applicable to like appeal when disposed of by the District Judge. From a reading of sub-section (1) it transpires that en appeal is to be filed before the District Judge and thereafter it could be transferred by the District Judge to a Subordinate Judge. So, the said Subordinate Judge hears the appeal having been vested with the same powers as that of the District Judge in the matter of hearing of the said appeal so transferred. So, from a reading of section 21(2) and 22 (3) of the Civil Court's Act it is clear that appeal from judgment or order passed by the Munsif shall lie to the District Judge and the District judge, on such appeal being filed before him, may hear it himself or may transfer the same to any subordinate Judge under his administrative control having competent jurisdiction to hear and dispose of the appeal and the Subordinate Judge has the same powers of the District Judge so far that appeal is concerned. As such, we find that the District Judge and the Subordinate Judge exercise concurrent jurisdiction in matters of appeal filed before the District Judge and subsequently transferred to a Subordinate Judge. So the District Judge has concurrent jurisdiction with the Subordinate Judge so far as that appeal, transferred to the Subordinate Judge. He does not hear the appeal in the exercise of his own jurisdiction. Unless an appeal is transferred to him the Subordinate Judge has no jurisdiction to hear an appeal. So, the Subordinate Judge while hearing the appeal is exercising the jurisdiction in accordance with the rules applicable to the disposal of the appeal by the District Judge. Thus, for purposes conceived in law the judgments and decrees or orders passed by the Subordinate judge on appeals transferred to him by the District Judge are to be understood and treated as judgments, decrees or orders passed by the District Judge himself. In that view of the matter the District Judge cannot entertain any revisional application against judgments, decrees or orders passed by the Subordinate Judge on appeal transferred by him to the Subordinate Judge. In my opinion, section 115(2) is not applicable to appeals which have been filed before the District Judge and which have been transferred by him to the Subordinate Judge for disposal. Appeals have been provided by section 96 of the Civil Procedure Code against decrees and under section 104 read with Order 43, rule 1 C.P.C. against the appealable orders. Section 96 states that an appeal shall lie from every decree passed by any court exercising original jurisdiction to the Court authorised to hear appeals from the decision of such Court and section 21(2) of the Civil Courts Act has clearly stated that an appeal from decree or order of the Munsif shall lie to the District Judge. So section 115 (2) of the Code of Civil Procedure or as introduced by the Law Reforms Ordinance does not apply to such cases. In the instant case, the learned Munsif rejected the prayer for temporary injunction in the exercise of his original jurisdiction. On appeal before the learned District Judge who was competent as the court of appeal to entertain the appeal, admitted the same and thereafter transferred the appeal to the court of the learned Subordinate Judge for disposal thereof. The learned Subordinate Judge who heard the appeal exercised jurisdiction as a court of appeal and disposed of the appeal transferred to him leaving no jurisdiction to be exercised by the learned District Judge on the consequence of the disposal of the appeal. In that view of the matter the preliminary objection as to the entertainment of the revisional application by the District judge is upheld and it is held that the application before the learned District Judge under section 115 (2) of the Code of Civil Procedure was not maintainable.
